text_blocks.snippet: Early signs of type 2 diabetes develop slowly over months or years, and some people show no symptoms at all.
snippet_highlighted_words: develop slowly over months or years

list.snippet: Increased thirst and frequent urination: High blood sugar forces your kidneys to work harder to filter and absorb excess glucose, pulling fluid from your tissues and causing you to pee more often—especially at night.
Constant fatigue: Your cells cannot absorb glucose properly to use as fuel, leaving you feeling tired and weak.
Increased hunger: Because your body’s cells are starved of energy, you may feel hungry even after eating.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar can cause fluid to shift into the lenses of your eyes or damage retinal blood vessels, making your sight blurry.
Slow-healing cuts and sores: High blood sugar impairs circulation and your immune system, making it harder for wounds to heal.
Tingling or numbness: Known as peripheral neuropathy, high blood sugar can damage nerves, often causing a pins-and-needles sensation or numbness in the hands and feet.

Darkened skin patches: A condition called acanthosis nigricans causes dark, velvety patches of skin to form in folds and creases (such as the neck, armpits, or groin), which signals insulin resistance.
Frequent infections: Higher sugar levels in the blood and urine can feed bacteria and yeast, leading to recurrent urinary tract or skin infections.
Unexplained weight loss: Though less common in type 2 than type 1, your body may start burning fat and muscle for energy if it cannot use glucose.
